items.value: A platform for accelerating the transition to net-zero, nature-positive food and water systems while building farmer resilience
items.reasoning: '100 Million Farmers' is a World Economic Forum initiative launched under its Food Action Alliance work, whose stated aim is to move food and water systems towards net-zero carbon and nature-positive production while raising the resilience and incomes of 100 million farmers by 2030. The other three options describe different things entirely: an organic animal husbandry network, a blockchain fertilizer trading exchange, and a farmer-producer-organisation market-access platform.

items.value: All four — battery storage, biomass generators, fuel cells and rooftop solar PV are all distributed energy resources
items.reasoning: Distributed Energy Resources are small-scale generation, storage or flexible-demand assets sited close to the point of consumption and connected at the distribution level rather than to the transmission grid. Rooftop solar photovoltaic units and small biomass generators are distributed generation; fuel cells are distributed generation as well; and battery storage is the standard example of distributed storage. All four appear in the conventional list of DERs, which also includes small wind, combined heat and power, backup generators, electric vehicles and demand response.

items.value: The fig, which is pollinated only by its coevolved fig wasp
items.reasoning: The fig (Ficus) and the fig wasp (family Agaonidae) form the textbook obligate mutualism: the fig's flowers are enclosed inside the syconium, which can be entered only by a female wasp of the matching species, and the wasp in turn can breed only inside a fig. Each fig species is typically served by its own wasp species, so no other insect can pollinate it. Mahua is pollinated by bats and a range of insects, sandalwood by generalist insects, and silk cotton chiefly by bats and birds.

items.value: All three groups — butterflies, fish and frogs — contain poisonous species
items.reasoning: Many butterflies are chemically defended: the monarch and its relatives sequester cardiac glycosides from the milkweeds their caterpillars eat, and advertise the fact with warning colours. Among fish, pufferfish and porcupinefish carry tetrodotoxin in their tissues and are lethal if eaten improperly. Among frogs, the poison dart frogs of Central and South America secrete batrachotoxin and other alkaloids through their skin. All three groups therefore include poisonous species.

items.value: Only one — red sanders is native to India; cashew and papaya are introduced species from tropical America
items.reasoning: Red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is endemic to a small tract of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh and grows naturally nowhere else in the world, so it is genuinely native to India. Cashew (Anacardium occidentale) is native to north-eastern Brazil and was brought to the Indian west coast by the Portuguese in the sixteenth century. Papaya (Carica papaya) is native to southern Mexico and Central America and reached India by the same Portuguese route. Only one of the three is Indian in origin.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; RTGs are not fission reactors but devices running on radioactive decay heat
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: a radioisotope thermoelectric generator has no chain reaction, no fuel assembly and no control rods — it simply converts the heat released by the natural decay of a radioisotope into electricity through thermocouples using the Seebeck effect. Statement 2 is correct, as RTGs have powered deep-space and planetary missions such as the Voyagers, Cassini, New Horizons, Curiosity and Perseverance, where sunlight is too weak or the nights too long for solar panels. Statement 3 is correct because the plutonium-238 they use is obtained by irradiating neptunium-237, which arises as a by-product of the plutonium production and reprocessing carried out for weapons programmes. Since statement 1 is false, every option except B is excluded.

items.value: Statement-I is incorrect — giant stars live much shorter lives than dwarfs — while Statement-II is correct
items.reasoning: Statement-I reverses the truth. Massive and giant stars consume their nuclear fuel prodigiously and last only millions of years, while small red dwarfs burn so slowly that their lifetimes run to hundreds of billions or trillions of years — longer than the present age of the universe. Statement-II is correct, and it is precisely the reason Statement-I is false: the far higher core temperatures and pressures of giant stars drive nuclear reactions at a much greater rate, so their much larger fuel supply is still exhausted far sooner.

items.value: Nitric oxide
items.reasoning: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesised in the body from the amino acid L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase, chiefly in the vascular endothelium. It diffuses into the underlying smooth muscle, raises cyclic GMP and relaxes the vessel wall, so it is the endothelium-derived relaxing factor that widens blood vessels and increases blood flow — the mechanism behind nitroglycerine in angina. Nitrous oxide is an inhaled anaesthetic, nitrogen dioxide is a toxic air pollutant, and nitrogen pentoxide is an unstable oxidising compound; none is made in the body as a vasodilator.

items.value: All three — radar can be used for concealed-substance screening at airports, for precipitation monitoring and for tracking animal migration
items.reasoning: Weather radar is the standard instrument for measuring rainfall intensity and movement, and Doppler weather radars also routinely detect and track migrating birds, bats and insects, which is the whole basis of radar ornithology and radar entomology — statements 2 and 3 are certain. For statement 1, the millimetre-wave and terahertz body scanners now used at airports are radar-based imaging systems that reveal objects concealed on a passenger or in an aircraft's structure, including narcotics packages, and terahertz spectroscopy can go further and identify the substance from its spectral signature. Runner-up is B (only two): B would win if the setter treated narcotics detection as belonging strictly to sniffer dogs, ion-mobility spectrometry and chemical swabs, and refused to count millimetre-wave screening as radar.

items.value: None of the three is a fifth generation fighter
items.reasoning: A fifth generation fighter is defined by all-aspect stealth shaping, internal weapons carriage, sensor fusion and networked situational awareness — the F-22, F-35, Su-57 and J-20 are the examples. The Rafale is a 4.5 generation multirole fighter with reduced but not low-observable signature. The MiG-29 is a fourth generation air-superiority fighter of the 1980s. Tejas Mk-1 is a fourth to 4.5 generation light combat aircraft; India's fifth generation programme is the still-developmental AMCA. The stem's spelling 'Rafael' appears to be a misprint for the Dassault 'Rafale' — Rafael is an Israeli defence firm, not an aircraft — but the answer is unaffected, since neither reading yields a fifth generation aircraft.

items.value: All three — hydrogels are used in controlled drug delivery, in air-conditioning and cooling systems, and in lubricant formulations
items.reasoning: Hydrogels are cross-linked hydrophilic polymer networks that swell in water without dissolving, and that structure is exploited in all three fields. In medicine they are the classic matrix for controlled and sustained drug release, swelling in response to pH, temperature or moisture to meter out a drug. In cooling, hydrogel desiccant and evaporative layers are used in compact and mobile air-conditioning and in atmospheric water-harvesting coolers because they can adsorb and release large amounts of water vapour. In tribology, the water held in a hydrogel network gives extremely low friction coefficients, which is why hydrogels are used as water-based lubricants and lubricating coatings. Runner-up is B (1 and 2 only): B would win if the setter regarded hydrogel lubrication as a laboratory curiosity rather than an established industrial lubricant application.

items.value: Water vapour
items.reasoning: In a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen supplied to the anode is split into protons and electrons; the electrons travel through the external circuit as the current that drives the motor, while the protons cross the electrolyte and combine at the cathode with oxygen from the air. The only product of that reaction is water, so the tailpipe emits water vapour and nothing else — which is why such vehicles are described as zero-emission at the point of use.

items.value: Long duration energy storage
items.reasoning: A pumped-storage hydropower plant has two reservoirs at different elevations. When electricity is cheap or surplus — typically at solar peak or overnight — water is pumped uphill; when demand peaks, it is released back down through turbines to generate power. It is therefore a way of storing energy in bulk for hours to days, and it remains by far the largest form of grid energy storage in the world, which is why it is discussed as the mainstay of long duration storage for balancing variable renewables. It is not an irrigation or rainwater-harvesting technique.

items.value: Wastewater treatment technologies
items.reasoning: A membrane bioreactor combines the biological treatment of the conventional activated sludge process with membrane filtration — microfiltration or ultrafiltration — in place of a secondary clarifier. The membrane retains the biomass completely, allowing much higher sludge concentrations, a smaller footprint and a high-quality effluent fit for reuse, which is why MBRs are now standard in compact urban sewage treatment and industrial effluent plants.

items.value: Money market
items.reasoning: Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation is a short-term instrument introduced by the Clearing Corporation of India that allows participants to borrow and lend funds against government securities placed as collateral, for tenors ranging from one day to a year. Being a secured short-term funds instrument settled through a central counterparty, it belongs to the money market alongside call money, notice money, treasury bills and commercial paper. It has since been largely replaced by TREPS, but its market classification is unchanged.

items.value: The average number of live births a woman would have by the end of her child-bearing age
items.reasoning: Total fertility rate is a synthetic measure: it sums the prevailing age-specific fertility rates to give the average number of children a woman would bear over her whole reproductive span if those rates persisted. Option A describes the crude birth rate, which is measured per thousand of the total population. Option C describes the rate of natural increase. Option B is close in spirit but is framed around a couple rather than a woman and omits the averaging that makes the measure a rate, so D is the precise definition.

items.value: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; NBFCs cannot access the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: the Liquidity Adjustment Facility, through which the RBI conducts repo and reverse repo operations, is open only to scheduled commercial banks (other than regional rural banks), primary dealers and certain other specified entities. Non-banking financial companies are not eligible counterparties, which is precisely why their liquidity stress in 2018-19 had to be addressed through indirect channels. Statement 2 is correct, since foreign institutional and portfolio investors are permitted to hold government securities within limits prescribed by the RBI and SEBI. Statement 3 is correct, as both the NSE and the BSE run dedicated debt market segments and platforms for trading bonds.

items.value: All three — insurance companies, pension funds and retail investors can all trade in corporate bonds and government securities
items.reasoning: Insurance companies and pension funds are among the largest institutional holders of both government securities and corporate bonds, since their long-dated liabilities are matched by such fixed-income assets and IRDAI and PFRDA investment norms actually require substantial allocations to them. Retail investors are also permitted access: they can buy listed corporate bonds through the exchanges' debt segments, and since the launch of the RBI Retail Direct scheme in 2021 they can open gilt accounts with the RBI and buy and sell government securities directly.

items.value: Only the exchange-traded fund and the currency swap are financial instruments; a motor vehicle is not
items.reasoning: A financial instrument is a contract that creates a financial asset for one party and a financial liability or equity claim for another. An exchange-traded fund is such an instrument — a tradable unit representing a claim on an underlying pool of securities. A currency swap is a derivative contract in which two parties exchange principal and interest streams in different currencies, so it too is a financial instrument. A motor vehicle is a physical or real asset used in production or consumption; it can be financed or leased, but the vehicle itself is not a financial contract.

items.value: Only two pairs are correct — dairy farm as primary and weaving cloth as secondary
items.reasoning: A dairy farm exploits a natural resource to produce a primary good, so pair 2 is correct, and weaving cloth transforms yarn into a manufactured product, so pair 4 is correct. Pair 1 is wrong: storage and warehousing do not make a new good, they support the movement and sale of goods already produced, and storage is listed with transport, trade, banking and communication as a tertiary or service sector activity. Pair 3 is wrong on the same logic in reverse: mining and the exploration of minerals are the extraction of a natural resource and belong to the primary sector, not the tertiary. Runner-up is C (only three): C would win if the setter treated 'mineral exploration' as a specialised professional service — which is how national accounting classifies exploration expenditure — rather than as part of mining.

items.value: All four — agricultural residues, corn grain, wastewater treatment sludge and wood mill waste can all serve as SAF feedstock
items.reasoning: Sustainable Aviation Fuel can be made by several certified pathways, and each of the four materials feeds one of them. Agricultural residues and wood mill waste are lignocellulosic biomass converted through gasification and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis or through alcohol-to-jet. Corn grain is fermented to ethanol which is then upgraded by the approved alcohol-to-jet route. Wastewater treatment sludge is a wet waste processed by hydrothermal liquefaction or by conversion of the volatile fatty acids it yields. All four appear on the standard published lists of SAF feedstocks. Runner-up is D (1, 3 and 4 only): D would win if the setter excluded corn grain on the ground that a food crop diverted to fuel fails the sustainability test that the word 'Sustainable' in SAF is meant to impose.

items.value: Only two pairs are correct — computer as fixed capital and petrol as working capital
items.reasoning: Fixed capital is the tools, machines and buildings that are used again and again over several years; working capital is the raw materials and cash that are used up in a single round of production. A computer is used repeatedly over years, so pair 2 is correct, and petrol is consumed as it is burnt, so pair 4 is correct. Pair 1 is wrong because a farmer's plough is a durable implement used season after season and is therefore fixed capital, not working capital. Pair 3 is wrong because yarn is the raw material that the weaver converts into cloth and is consumed in the process, making it working capital rather than fixed capital.

items.value: Metaverse
items.reasoning: The metaverse is precisely the idea described: a persistent, interoperable network of three-dimensional virtual worlds accessible simultaneously by very large numbers of users, in which participants can own, buy and sell virtual land, avatars and objects as property, often recorded as non-fungible tokens. Big data analytics is the extraction of patterns from large datasets, cryptography is the mathematics of securing information, and 'virtual matrix' is not a recognised term for this concept.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — there is a minimum capital requirement for a wholly owned subsidiary, but the 50 per cent Indian-national board rule does apply
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong. Under the RBI's 2013 scheme for the setting up of wholly owned subsidiaries by foreign banks, a WOS must have an initial minimum paid-up voting equity capital or net worth of Rs 500 crore, so a minimum capital requirement plainly exists. Statement 2 reflects the governance conditions of the same scheme, which require that at least half the directors on the WOS board be Indian nationals resident in India, with a further stipulation on non-executive and independent directors. Runner-up is D (neither correct): D would win if the board-composition threshold were in fact set at a level other than one-half — the condition also carries residency and independence riders — in which case statement 2 as printed would fail too.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct — CSR rules do exclude spending that benefits the company or its employees, and they do prescribe a minimum spend of two per cent
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules expressly exclude from CSR any activity that benefits only the employees of the company and their families, and more generally any expenditure undertaken in the normal course of the company's own business, so a spend that benefits the company directly does not qualify. Statement 2 is wrong: section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company falling within the prescribed net worth, turnover or net profit thresholds to spend at least two per cent of its average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years on CSR, and unspent amounts must be transferred to a specified fund or an Unspent CSR Account.
